mcqs.question: Why does encoding the inverse operation directly on each Command object, rather than in a separate history/snapshot structure, matter?
options: It makes the Command interface simpler to compile
The forward and inverse operations live together on the same object, so they can never drift out of sync as the codebase evolves
It removes the need for a CommandHistory stack entirely
It's required because interfaces cannot reference external state
mcqs.explanation: Keeping execute() and undo() on the same object means any change to the forward operation forces the author to reconsider the inverse right there, preventing drift. It doesn't affect compilation, a history stack is still needed to track order, and interfaces referencing state is a non-issue.

mcqs.question: In MacroCommand, why must undo() iterate the wrapped commands in reverse order from how execute() ran them?
options: Reverse iteration is required by the Command interface's method signature
It reduces the number of commands that need to be stored in memory
A later command may depend on an earlier one having already run, so undoing must reverse the later command's effect before the earlier one's
It makes the macro command execute faster on the next run
mcqs.explanation: If command B assumed A had already executed, undoing A before B could leave the system in an inconsistent state — reversing in the opposite order of execution respects those dependencies. Nothing about the interface signature forces this, memory usage is unaffected, and it has no bearing on execution speed.

mcqs.question: What's the right way to handle an action that has no true inverse, like an email that's already been delivered?
options: Force a fake undo() that silently does nothing, so the API stays consistent
Delete the sent email from the recipient's inbox programmatically
Automatically retry sending it, hoping the second send corrects the first
Model undo as a compensating action if one exists, like a follow-up disregard notice, or don't offer undo for that action at all
mcqs.explanation: When no true reversal exists, the honest options are a compensating action or no undo — pretending undo() succeeded, or reaching into a system you don't control, just hides the problem. Retrying the send doesn't correct anything and isn't a form of undo at all.

mcqs.question: Why is implementing undo as "re-run every command from scratch except the last one" a poor design?
options: It's O(n) per undo instead of O(1), and it breaks the moment any command has a side effect, like sending a notification, that shouldn't fire again on replay
It requires every command to be serializable to disk
It makes the CommandHistory stack unnecessary
It's actually the standard, correct way undo is implemented in most editors
mcqs.explanation: Replaying history is both slower than a direct per-command undo and unsafe for any command with an external side effect that can't safely re-fire. It has nothing to do with serialization, a history structure is still needed, and this is a known anti-pattern, not the standard approach.
